title: The history of the transistor, from 1947 to the first microprocessor
summary: Follow the people, institutions and manufacturing ideas that converged in a CPU on a chip.

blocks.heading: Three branches converge
blocks.alt: A relationship map links Bell Labs transistor work and its MOS branch, Texas Instruments integrated-circuit work, and Fairchild planar-process and integration work to Intel’s 4004 collaboration with Busicom. Arrows denote technological contributions rather than every employment move.
blocks.caption: Selective dependency map, 1947–1971. Dates inside the nodes anchor the history; arrows express the contributions discussed below.

blocks.heading: Start with a question, then follow a branch
blocks.body: How did one experimental amplifier become an entire processor? Device physics made switching possible, manufacturing made repeated structures dependable, and architecture made those structures useful as a programmable machine. The map separates those contributions so “smaller transistors” does not stand in for the whole explanation.

blocks.heading: Bell Labs: making a solid-state device work
rows: John Bardeen and Walter Brattain · 1947
Point-contact transistor action in germanium
A semiconductor device could amplify
William Shockley and the Bell Labs program
Junction-transistor development after the point-contact breakthrough
The laboratory result opened multiple device paths
Mohamed Atalla and Dawon Kahng · 1959 work, 1960 demonstration
MOS field-effect device using a silicon/oxide interface
An insulated gate offered another way to control a channel
blocks.caption: The branches are related but not identical: the 1947 point-contact device was not a miniature MOSFET.

blocks.heading: The surface appears twice for a reason
blocks.body: Atalla and Kahng’s branch depends on controlling the silicon/oxide interface so a field can influence the channel. Hoerni’s planar branch uses oxide to protect junctions and support fabrication from the wafer surface. The shared material matters, but the two contributions solve different immediate problems.

blocks.heading: Two routes into integration
rows: Texas Instruments · Jack Kilby · 1958
Demonstrated an integrated circuit in semiconductor material
A circuit could be built together rather than assembled solely from separate components
Fairchild · Jean Hoerni · 1959
Planar manufacturing process
Protected junctions and a practical surface for repeated processing
Fairchild · Robert Noyce · 1959
Planar monolithic circuit concept with interconnection
A manufacturable route for connecting components on one chip
Fairchild · Jay Last and team · 1960
Fabricated a planar integrated circuit
The manufacturing idea became working circuit hardware

blocks.heading: Do not flatten independent work into a single handoff
blocks.body: Kilby’s demonstration and Noyce’s planar approach were distinct contributions. Drawing one arrow from TI to Fairchild would incorrectly suggest a simple transfer in which the second merely received the first. The map instead shows two branches contributing to the integrated-circuit story.

blocks.heading: Intel and Busicom: the processor becomes a project
rows: Architecture and system concept
Ted Hoff and Stan Mazor
A programmable approach addressed the calculator project
Silicon design and implementation
Federico Faggin, working with Masatoshi Shima
A concept needed detailed circuitry, layout and a working implementation
Calculator requirements and collaboration
Busicom and Shima
The customer problem helped shape the chip set
Commercial milestone · 1971
Intel 4004
A CPU on one chip, within a supporting multi-chip system
blocks.caption: The 4004 is commonly identified as the first commercially available general-purpose single-chip microprocessor. Earlier and contemporary processor efforts make an unqualified “first processor” claim too broad.

blocks.heading: A CPU on one chip was not the whole computer
blocks.body: The 4004 did not eliminate the need for program storage, data storage, interfaces and the rest of the system. Integration changes a boundary: more of the processor function sits inside one package. It does not make every surrounding function disappear.

slides.title: If your question is device physics
slides.body: Follow Bell Labs → transistor → MOS. Ask what controls current and what the gate is insulated from. The visible device shape is less important than the mechanism.

slides.title: If your question is manufacturing
slides.body: Follow Fairchild → planar process → monolithic IC. Ask what can be repeated, protected and connected across a wafer. A working specimen and a repeatable process are different achievements.

slides.title: If your question is computing
slides.body: Follow integrated circuits + MOS + architecture → 4004. Ask which function moved onto the chip and which remained outside it. The answer is a system boundary, not just a transistor count.

blocks.heading: Read the arrows
blocks.prompt: Why are the planar process and CPU architecture separate branches?
options: They are competing names for the same invention
One concerns making structures and connections; the other concerns organizing computation
blocks.explanation: Manufacturing capability does not by itself specify an instruction set or processor organization. Architecture without an implementable process does not produce a chip.
